title: Move Like the Greats
tagline: Study the GOATs, see the springs, steal what you can use.
intro_markdown:
Watch Usain Bolt run, Lionel Messi dribble or Bruce Lee shift his weight, and you see something a stopwatch or a bench-press number can't measure. They look **relaxed, springy and connected**, as if every part of the body is working on the same job.

This module is about learning to see that. We'll study a handful of the greatest movers in sport, one at a time, through two lenses:

- **The fascia lens** from **Chong Xie**, author of *Secret of Athleticism* and creator of the Hyperarch Fascia Training system. He separates athletes into "fascia-driven" and "muscle-driven" movers, and he reads athleticism from the feet up.
- **The movement-pattern lens** from **GOATA**, a system built on slow-motion study of durable movers. Coaches like **Nick Ball**, an ACE-certified trainer who describes himself as a GOATA specialist, teach it as simple daily practice.

Then we add what sport science has actually measured: tendons that act like catapults, arches that act like springs, and Bolt's ground contacts lasting less than a tenth of a second.

One ground rule runs through this module. **We talk about athletes as individuals.** Each of these people built their movement through their own childhood play, training, injuries and habits. None of it comes from belonging to a group.

For every athlete you'll get three things:
1. **What to watch**: foot strike, relaxation, rotation, elastic rebound.
2. **Footage and breakdowns**, embedded right here.
3. **What you can borrow**, at home, with no equipment.

The last lesson is a placeholder for the most personal breakdown in the course. It's Josh's own movement, analysed the same way once his footage is uploaded.

> A note on honesty: the coaches here hold strong views, and so does Josh. When something is their philosophy or lived experience, we say so. When it's measured science, we cite it. Both matter, and they aren't the same thing.

lessons.title: How to Watch a GOAT: Fascia-Driven vs Muscle-Driven
lessons.summary: Before we study individual athletes, learn the lens: what 'fascia-driven' movement looks like, what science says about elastic recoil, and the four things to watch in any great mover.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Two athletes, same jump

Picture two athletes who jump the same height. One looks like he's working hard: big wind-up, tight face, a grind on the way up. The other just seems to *pop* off the floor, with a loose face, quiet arms and a soft landing.

Chong Xie, author of *Secret of Athleticism* and creator of the Hyperarch Fascia Training system, has built his work around that difference. The show notes for his Just Fly Performance podcast episode put it simply: "There is a big difference between athletes where the power is coming from the fascia vs. an athlete where the power is coming from the muscle." He calls the first group **fascia-driven** and the second **muscle-driven**.

This is Josh's starting point too. The greats don't look effortless because they aren't trying. They look effortless because **a large share of their power comes from elastic tissue, not just from squeezing muscle harder.**

## What the science actually shows

You don't have to take this on faith. Several pieces of solid research point in the same direction.

- **Tendons work like catapults.** In a 2002 study in the *Journal of Physiology*, Kawakami and colleagues used ultrasound on the calf during an ankle movement with a counter-movement (a dip before you push). The muscle fibres worked *almost isometrically*, holding length like a clamp, while the tendon took on the job of storing and releasing elastic energy.
- **Springs are everywhere in the leg.** A review by Roberts and Azizi (2011, *Journal of Experimental Biology*) describes how the muscles that power vertebrate movement work alongside springy tissue, both inside the muscle and in connective tissue such as tendons. It argues that these springs let the body operate beyond what muscle alone can do.
- **Your arch is a spring.** A 1987 paper in *Nature* by Ker, Alexander and colleagues showed that the arch of the human foot stores and returns elastic energy when you run.
- **The "lines" are real, at least in parts.** Jan Wilke's 2016 systematic review tested Tom Myers' myofascial meridians against dissection studies. It found strong evidence for continuous connective-tissue links in three lines: the superficial back line (from the sole of the foot up the back of the body) and the front and back functional lines (crossing diagonally through the trunk). It found moderate-to-strong evidence for parts of the spiral and lateral lines, and none for the superficial front line. The authors said that working out what these chains *do* during movement is the most urgent task for future research.

So here is the honest version. Elastic recoil is real and measured. Whole-body fascial connections are partly mapped. The idea that the greats are mainly *fascia-driven* is a coaching model that fits the evidence well, but no one has proven it in a lab. Hold it as a powerful lens, not a law.

## The GOATA angle

GOATA reaches a similar place from a different direction. It was founded by **José Guillermo "Gil" Boesch**, and its lead coaches include **Gary Scheffler** and **Ricky Stanzi**, a former Iowa quarterback. Boesch built the system by studying slow-motion video of athletes, children and older adults, and concluded that high-level athletes shared the same movement patterns. Stanzi has described the approach in one line: "We're just watching the most durable humans on the planet." His slow-motion breakdowns range from amateurs to stars like Michael Jordan.

The acronym stands for "Greatest Of All Time **Athletes**". The core idea is simple: **the greats share movement patterns, and you can re-learn them.**

One fair warning. Independent research on GOATA is thin. Even a friendly overview on *Mundo Entrenamiento* notes that its scientific validation "is still developing." Use it like a coach's eye, not a lab result.

## The four things to watch

For every athlete in this module, train your eye on four signals.

1. **Foot strike and the arch.** Where does the foot land? Does it look stiff and springy, or soft and collapsing? Chong Xie reads elite feet for tension. He has said "the toes of elite athletes are like claws, very stiff" and that "elite athletes are made naturally from the difference in tension in the foot."
2. **Relaxation.** Watch the face, the jaw, the hands and the shoulders. Tension in those places usually means the athlete is muscling the movement.
3. **Rotation.** Great movers turn from the ground up through the hips, ribs and shoulders, with no break in the chain.
4. **Elastic rebound.** Is there a brief, bouncy contact and then a release? Or a long, grinding push?

## What you can borrow today: the 30-second watch drill

### How to do it
Pick any clip in this module. Watch it four times, and each time look at **only one** of the four signals. Say out loud what you see: "Stiff foot. Loose jaw. Hips lead. Short bounce."

### Sets & timing
One clip a day, four viewings, about two minutes.

### Why it works
You can't copy what you can't see. Chong Xie and the GOATA coaches built their systems by studying footage of great movers. This drill is the beginner's version of the same habit.

### Common mistakes
- Trying to see everything at once. One signal per viewing.
- Only watching the highlight moment. Watch the **steps before** the dunk, the sprint or the strike.
- Assuming every great athlete moves the same way. Look for the shared principle, not a carbon copy.
key_takeaways: Chong Xie distinguishes 'fascia-driven' athletes, who get much of their power from elastic tissue, from 'muscle-driven' ones.

Measured science supports the pieces: tendons recoil like catapults (Kawakami 2002), the foot arch is a spring (Ker et al. 1987), and three myofascial lines have strong anatomical evidence (Wilke 2016).

GOATA was founded by José Guillermo 'Gil' Boesch, with coaches including Gary Scheffler and Ricky Stanzi. It is based on slow-motion study of durable movers, and its independent evidence base is still thin.
Watch every athlete for four signals: foot strike, relaxation, rotation and elastic rebound.

lessons.title: Usain Bolt: The Relaxed Spring
lessons.summary: The fastest human ever timed looked like he was cruising. Here's what the biomechanics show about Bolt's ground contact, his asymmetry and his relaxation, and what you can borrow.
lessons.body_markdown:
## The man who smiled at full speed

Berlin, 2009: 9.58 seconds, the 100m world record. Watch the footage and something feels off. Bolt doesn't look like he's straining. In some races he famously eased up before the line.

That look of effortlessness is the whole point of this lesson. **The faster you want to go, the less you can afford to fight yourself.**

## What the numbers say

Bolt is one of the most studied sprinters in history, so we can look at real data.

- **Ground contact under a tenth of a second.** Čoh and colleagues (2018, *Kinesiology*) analysed Bolt's 9.85s run at the 2011 World Challenge meeting in Zagreb. At top speed his foot was on the ground for about **86 milliseconds**, then he was airborne for about **145 milliseconds**. Peak vertical force hit about **4.2 times his body weight**, and his centre of mass moved up and down only about **4.9 cm**. In their summary: a relatively long stride, a minimal braking phase and minimal vertical bounce.
- **A softer spring than his rivals.** Taylor and Beneke (2012, *International Journal of Sports Medicine*) modelled Bolt, Tyson Gay and Asafa Powell as spring-mass systems, using data from the 2009 World Championships in Berlin. Bolt was fastest over 60–80m, at about 12.3 m/s, yet his estimated leg stiffness was *significantly lower* than theirs. His ground contact was longer and his step frequency lower. He covered the ground with fewer, longer, springy bounds.
- **Asymmetry he didn't "fix".** According to his autobiography, Bolt has scoliosis, and his right leg is about half an inch shorter than his left. In 2017, researchers in Peter Weyand's lab at Southern Methodist University (led by Andrew Udofa) analysed race video. They estimated that his right leg hit the track with about 13% more peak force, while his left stayed down about 14% longer. Weyand's view: "correcting his asymmetry would not speed him up and might even slow him down." These were early, video-based findings presented at a conference, not a final paper.

## The fascia lens

Chong Xie has made a whole video on recreating "Usain Bolt's feet and fascia connection." In his view, Bolt's speed starts with the tension and spring in his feet, travels up a connected chain into the glutes, and is expressed with a relaxed upper body.

GOATA coaches read Bolt in a similar way. One GOATA coach's front-view breakdown contrasts Bolt's "decompressed" form with a stiff sprinter.

Josh's take is that this is what fascia-driven looks like at the highest level. The body is long, loose and springy, and the work is done by the bounce, not the grind.

## What to watch

1. **Foot strike:** Watch slow-motion footage. The foot lands under the body, not far in front, and leaves almost immediately.
2. **Relaxation:** Look at the jaw, cheeks and hands. They're loose, even at over 12 m/s.
3. **Rotation:** The shoulders and hips counter-rotate smoothly. Nothing is locked.
4. **Elastic rebound:** Very little up-and-down. The bounce sends him forward, not upward.

## What you can borrow: relaxed strides

You don't need a track or spikes.

### How to do it
1. Warm up with 2–3 minutes of easy jogging and some light skipping. Chong Xie notes that "for elite athletes, the fascial system takes time to warm up", so don't skip this.
2. Run 60–80m strides at about 70–80% effort.
3. On each stride, choose one cue: **loose jaw**, **loose hands** (thumb resting lightly on the index finger), or **quick, quiet feet**.
4. Walk back slowly. Full recovery between reps.

### Sets & timing
4–6 strides, two or three times a week, after a proper warm-up.

### Why it works
The research above shows elite speed coming from short, springy ground contacts with little wasted bounce. Tension in your face, neck and hands tends to stiffen the whole chain. Relaxing is a skill, and strides are where you practise it.

### Common mistakes
- **Sprinting flat out.** Relaxation disappears at max effort until you've grooved it at sub-max speeds.
- **Reaching with the foot.** Overstriding increases braking. Let the foot land under you.
- **Trying to copy Bolt's asymmetry.** His stride suits *his* body. Borrow the principle (relaxed, springy, connected), not the quirks.
- **Skipping the warm-up.** Cold tissue is less springy and more vulnerable.
key_takeaways: At top speed Bolt's foot was on the ground for about 86 ms, with only about 4.9 cm of vertical bounce (Čoh et al. 2018).
Bolt ran faster than his rivals with lower estimated leg stiffness, using longer, springier bounds (Taylor & Beneke 2012).
Bolt's scoliosis and stride asymmetry may suit his body. SMU researchers suggested 'fixing' it might slow him down.
Chong Xie and GOATA coaches both read Bolt as relaxed, connected and elastic from the feet up.
Borrow the principle with relaxed sub-maximal strides: loose jaw, loose hands, quick quiet feet.

lessons.title: Messi & Ronaldinho: Feet That Talk to the Ground
lessons.summary: Two of football's most magical dribblers, studied for low balance, quick light feet and joyful, playful movement, plus the barefoot and futsal roots Chong Xie loves to talk about.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Small steps, big magic

Sprinters run in a straight line. Footballers have to accelerate, brake, cut, feint and keep the ball glued to their feet, all at once, while someone tries to knock them over.

Two players became symbols of doing this beautifully: **Lionel Messi** and **Ronaldinho**. Their styles were very different. What they shared was a feeling of being *light* on the ground and *connected* through the body.

## Lionel Messi: low, quick, unbothered

Some facts first. Messi was diagnosed with a growth hormone deficiency at age 10. As a teenager he was physically weaker than his opponents, and he worked to build muscle and strength. Wikipedia's summary of his style points to a **low centre of gravity** and the **balance** it gives him to withstand challenges. It also notes that his **short, strong legs** allow short bursts of acceleration, and that his **quick feet** let him keep control of the ball at speed. Diego Maradona put it more simply: "The ball stays glued to his foot."

Chong Xie has a video titled *"Messi is Fascia Driven not Muscle Driven."* The title says it all. In his view, Messi's power and balance come less from big muscles and more from springy, tensioned feet and a connected chain up through the hips.

## Ronaldinho: the joy of the ground

Ronaldinho developed an interest in **futsal** and **beach football** before organised football. Wikipedia notes that many of his signature moves come from futsal, especially his ball control. Futsal is played on a hard court with a smaller, heavier ball, and it rewards quick touches and constant foot-ball contact.

Chong Xie has made a video on *"The Story of Ronaldinho and His Barefoot Training."* For him, a childhood spent playing barefoot and on varied surfaces builds feet that stay strong, sensitive and springy. In his view, that's the foundation of a fascia-driven athlete.

This connects to the core of Josh's philosophy. The best movers often built their bodies **through play**: varied ground, bare feet, endless touches. Machines and isolated muscle work came much later, if at all.

## What to watch

1. **Foot strike:** Lots of short, quick contacts, mostly on the front of the foot. The heel rarely sticks.
2. **Relaxation:** Messi's upper body stays quiet while his feet work. Ronaldinho is famously loose and smiling.
3. **Rotation:** Watch the hips turn *before* the shoulders on a cut. The body moves as one coil.
4. **Elastic rebound:** After contact from a defender, they bounce back to balance rather than stumbling.

## What you can borrow: barefoot ground time and quick feet

### How to do it
**Part A: barefoot ground time.** On a safe surface (grass, sand, a clean floor), walk barefoot for a few minutes. Feel the ground through the whole foot: heel, outside edge, ball, toes. Then do light, quick on-the-spot steps, staying on the balls of the feet.

**Part B: quick-feet touches.** With a ball (any ball), do sole rolls and alternating toe-taps for 20–30 seconds. Keep your upper body relaxed and your eyes up when you can.

### Sets & timing
Part A: 3–5 minutes daily. Part B: 3–4 rounds of 20–30 seconds, a few times a week.

### Why it works
Your foot is a sensory organ as well as a spring. The arch stores and returns energy (Ker et al., 1987). Chong Xie argues that foot tension sits at the base of athletic movement. Varied, barefoot, playful contact is the closest adult version of how these players grew up.

### Common mistakes
- **Going from shoes to long barefoot runs overnight.** Build up gradually. Feet that have lived in shoes need time to adapt.
- **Stomping.** Aim for quiet, quick contacts.
- **Stiff upper body.** If your shoulders creep up, slow down until they drop.
- **Unsafe surfaces.** Check for glass and sharp objects first.
key_takeaways: Messi's style is widely described in terms of a low centre of gravity, balance, quick feet and short bursts of acceleration.
Chong Xie argues that Messi is 'fascia-driven', getting balance and power from springy feet and a connected chain rather than big muscles.
Ronaldinho grew up drawn to futsal and beach football, and many of his signature moves trace back to futsal.
The shared lesson is that the best movers often built their bodies through varied, playful, often barefoot contact with the ground.
Borrow it with gradual barefoot ground time and quick-feet ball touches, keeping the upper body relaxed.

lessons.title: LeBron, Jordan & Kobe: Durability, Landing and a Quiet Mind
lessons.summary: Basketball's greats jumped and landed thousands of times a season for two decades. We look at LeBron's record longevity, Jordan on the balls of his feet, Kobe's mindfulness, and the fascia view of each.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Jumping for twenty years

Basketball is brutal on the body. You sprint, stop, cut, jump and land, again and again, on a hard floor for years. Staying great in that sport is as much about **durability** as talent.

## LeBron James: the longevity case

LeBron holds NBA records for the most seasons played (24), the most games and the most minutes. At the time of writing he is also the league's oldest active player. For much of his career he stayed remarkably healthy. Wikipedia describes a groin injury in the 2018–19 season as "the first major injury of his career", and it came more than 15 years in. He has had other injuries since, including ankle and foot problems, so he isn't injury-proof. But his availability over two decades is extraordinary.

Through this course's fascia lens, the question is what his body does every time it lands. Chong Xie's core argument, laid out in the long interview below, is that strong, tensioned, springy feet absorb and return force and spare the knees, hips and back above them. That's a coaching view, not a measured explanation of LeBron's career. Durability has many parts: sleep, recovery, load management and genetics as well as movement quality.

## Michael Jordan: living on the balls of the feet

GOATA coach Ricky Stanzi's slow-motion breakdowns have included Michael Jordan. One GOATA coach's clip highlights Jordan playing defence while moving on the balls of his feet: low, springy and ready. On the Just Fly podcast, Chong Xie also used Jordan as an example, discussing why some elite players let their knees come together while shooting and how that relates to glute activation.

What stands out when you watch Jordan is how *loaded* he always looks. The heels are light, the hips are back, and he's ready to bounce in any direction.

## Kobe Bryant: the calm engine

Not everything about elite movement is physical. **George Mumford**, a mindfulness teacher, spent five years working with Phil Jackson's Bulls, then followed Jackson to the Lakers in 1999. The *Boston Globe* reported that Mumford "helped turn Kobe Bryant into an outspoken adherent of meditation." Kobe's endorsement of Mumford's book *The Mindful Athlete* says: "George helped me understand the art of mindfulness... I learned just to be."

This ties straight into the holistic side of this course. A calm nervous system lets the body move freely, while an anxious one tightens everything. Body, mind and soul are one system.

## What to watch

1. **Foot strike:** On defence and before a jump, watch the heels. Are they light? Is the weight on the front of the foot?
2. **Relaxation:** Kobe's and Jordan's faces before a big shot are often strikingly calm.
3. **Rotation:** On a drive, the hips and shoulders turn as one unit off a planted foot.
4. **Elastic rebound:** Watch the landings. The greats land soft and quiet, then go again.

## What you can borrow: soft landings and a calm breath

### How to do it
**Soft-landing hops:** Stand tall. Do small, quick hops on the spot, landing on the balls of the feet with the heels kissing the ground lightly. Make each landing as **quiet** as possible. Progress to small hops forward and back, then side to side.

**Calm breath reset:** Before each set, take three slow breaths through the nose, with a long, easy exhale. Let your shoulders drop.

### Sets & timing
3 sets of 15–20 small hops, resting 60 seconds, 2–3 times a week. Breath reset before every set.

### Why it works
Schleip and Müller's 2013 review of fascial training principles lists **elastic recoil**, meaning bouncy, springy loading, as a core way to train connective tissue. They suggest training once or twice a week, with a more resilient "fascial body suit" building over 6–24 months. Quiet landings teach you to absorb force through a springy chain instead of jarring into your joints. The breath work borrows from the Kobe and Mumford lesson that a calm mind lets the body move freely.

### Common mistakes
- **Big, heavy jumps.** Start small. The goal is spring, not height.
- **Landing flat-footed or with locked knees.** Land on the front of the foot with a slight, springy bend.
- **Doing too much too soon.** Fascia and tendons adapt slowly. Build over weeks.
- **Ignoring pain.** Sharp pain means stop. If you have a current injury, check with a qualified professional before hopping.
key_takeaways: LeBron holds NBA records for most seasons, games and minutes, and his first major injury came more than 15 years into his career.
Chong Xie argues that strong, springy feet protect everything above them. Applied to LeBron, that's a coaching lens, not a proven explanation.
GOATA coaches study Jordan in slow motion, highlighting how he moved on the balls of his feet.
Kobe Bryant practised mindfulness with George Mumford, a reminder that a calm nervous system is part of athletic movement.
Borrow it with quiet, springy hops and a slow-breath reset, and build up gradually because connective tissue adapts over months.

lessons.title: Bruce Lee, Muhammad Ali & Zhang Weili: Be Water
lessons.summary: Combat sports show the elastic body under pressure: Bruce Lee's 'be water', Ali's dancing footwork, and Zhang Weili, a UFC champion who lists Chong Xie among her trainers.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Power that doesn't look like effort

In combat sports, tension costs you twice. A tense fighter is slower, and easier to read. The great strikers move like they're made of rubber and hit like they're made of iron.

## Bruce Lee: "Be water"

On 9 December 1971, *The Pierre Berton Show* aired what became Bruce Lee's only English-language TV interview, later released as *The Lost Interview*. Two words from it, **"be water"**, became so famous that ESPN's *30 for 30* documentary about him is titled *Be Water*.

The idea is formless adaptability: water takes the shape of whatever holds it, and it can flow or crash. For this course, it's also a perfect picture of fascia-driven movement. You stay loose and fluid until the moment of impact, then the whole body connects.

## Muhammad Ali: float, then sting

"Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee." The line came from a poem by Ali's cornerman and speechwriter **Drew "Bundini" Brown**, and Ali recited it at a press conference before his February 1964 fight with Sonny Liston. The breakdown below, from *The Modern Martial Artist*, takes apart Ali's footwork and jab.

Watch Ali's feet. He's up on the balls of the feet, bouncing, never planted flat for long. That's elastic rebound on display: a rhythmic, springy base that lets him change direction instantly.

## Zhang Weili: the fascia coach in the corner

This is where the module meets its primary source directly. On **31 August 2019**, Zhang Weili stopped Jéssica Andrade **42 seconds** into the first round to win the UFC strawweight title. She became the first UFC champion from China and the first from Asia.

Zhang's Wikipedia profile lists **Chong Xie of Hyperarch Fascia Training** among her trainers, and Chong describes his role as movement and fascia conditioning coach. He has posted videos from their work together, including one on increasing punching power. A world title has many contributors, and her head coaches and team did most of the work. But it's a striking example of fascia training at the very top of a sport.

His point is that a punch starts at the floor. Force has to travel from the foot, through the hip and trunk, and out through the fist. Any weak link, often the foot, leaks power.

## What to watch

1. **Foot strike:** Weight on the balls of the feet, constant small adjustments.
2. **Relaxation:** Loose shoulders and hands until impact. Watch Lee and Ali between exchanges.
3. **Rotation:** On a power shot, the hip turns first and the shoulder and fist follow, like a whip.
4. **Elastic rebound:** Ali's bounce is the clearest example of rhythmic, springy loading you'll see in any sport.

## What you can borrow: the fighter's bounce and ground-up rotation

### How to do it
**Fighter's bounce:** Stand with feet about hip-width apart, knees softly bent. Bounce lightly on the balls of the feet, keeping the heels just off the floor and your shoulders loose. Add small steps forward, back and side to side, staying light.

**Ground-up rotation:** From a staggered stance, slowly turn as if throwing a punch. **Start the turn by pressing the back foot into the floor**, let the hip follow, then the ribs, then the shoulder and arm. Keep the arm relaxed. Do it slowly first, then a little faster, always relaxed.

### Sets & timing
Bounce: 3 rounds of 60 seconds with 30 seconds of rest. Rotation: 2 sets of 10 slow reps on each side. Do both 2–3 times a week.

### Why it works
Rhythmic bouncing is the elastic-recoil principle from Schleip and Müller's fascial training framework. Ground-up rotation trains the sequence through the crossing diagonal "functional lines" that Wilke's 2016 review found strong anatomical evidence for. These lines connect one side of the trunk to the opposite hip and leg.

### Common mistakes
- **Bouncing flat-footed.** Stay on the front of the foot with light heels.
- **Muscling the arm.** The arm is the end of the whip, not the motor.
- **Holding your breath.** Breathe out on the rotation.
- **Rushing speed.** Get the sequence right slowly before adding speed or a bag.
key_takeaways: Bruce Lee's 'be water', from his 1971 Pierre Berton interview, is a perfect picture of loose-until-impact, fascia-driven movement.
'Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee' came from a poem by Drew 'Bundini' Brown, and Ali's springy, bouncing footwork shows it.
Zhang Weili won the UFC strawweight title in 42 seconds in 2019. Chong Xie is listed among her trainers as her fascia coach.
Power travels from the ground up through the foot, hip, trunk and fist, along diagonal connections with strong anatomical evidence.
Borrow it with a light fighter's bounce and slow, relaxed ground-up rotations.

lessons.body_markdown:
## Why this lesson exists

Everything in this module has been about learning to *see* great movement. This lesson turns the camera around. Josh, the founder of this course, spent years dealing with chronic injuries and expensive physio. He rebuilt his body through simple, at-home fascia work. By his own account he hasn't needed a physio visit since around 2021–22, while training harder than ever.

That's Josh's lived experience, not a clinical trial. But it's exactly why the course exists, and footage is the most honest way to show it.

> **Status:** waiting on video. This lesson will be written once Josh uploads footage.

## What we'll film (suggested shot list)

For fair comparison with the athletes in this module, we'd ideally get:

1. **Barefoot walking:** side view and front view, 10–15 steps each.
2. **Relaxed strides:** side view, 60–80m at about 70–80% effort (as in the Bolt lesson). Slow motion if possible (120fps or more on most phones).
3. **Soft-landing hops:** side and front view, 15 small hops (as in the basketball lesson).
4. **Fighter's bounce and ground-up rotation:** front and 45-degree view (as in the combat lesson).
5. **A sport-specific movement** of Josh's choice: cutting, jumping, kicking, throwing or anything else that shows how he moves when it counts.
6. **Any "before" footage**, if it exists, from the injury years. Even a few seconds would be powerful.

Filming tips: steady phone at hip height, good light, tight-fitting or minimal clothing so the joints are visible, and the whole body in frame.

## What we'll analyse

We'll use the same **four signals** applied to every athlete in this module:

1. **Foot strike and arch:** Where does the foot land? How long is ground contact? Does the arch look springy or collapsing?
2. **Relaxation:** Jaw, hands, shoulders. Where does tension show up, and where doesn't it?
3. **Rotation:** Does movement start from the ground and flow through the hip, trunk and shoulder in sequence?
4. **Elastic rebound:** Is there a short, springy bounce, or a long push?

Where useful, we'll put Josh's clips side by side with the athlete footage from earlier lessons. The goal isn't to claim he moves like Bolt. It's to show what these principles look like in an everyday athlete's body.

## What we'll pair it with

- **Josh's story:** the injuries, where they were, what physio cost him, what changed, and when. (A separate interview will capture this in Josh's own words.)
- **His daily practice:** the exact simple drills he does at home.
- **Honest framing:** what Josh *believes* (for example, that healthy fascia makes injury extremely unlikely) clearly labelled as his philosophy and experience, alongside what the research does and doesn't show.

## For now: try it on yourself

### How to do it
Film yourself doing items 1–3 from the shot list above. Watch each clip four times, looking at one signal per viewing.

### Sets & timing
Once now, then again after 6–8 weeks of the drills in this module.

### Why it works
Schleip and Müller suggest a more resilient fascial body builds over 6–24 months. Video is the simplest way to see slow change that you can't feel day to day.

### Common mistakes
- Judging yourself against elite athletes. Compare **you to you**.
- Filming from different angles each time. Keep the setup the same so comparisons are fair.
key_takeaways: This lesson will analyse Josh's own movement with the same four-signal lens used on the greats.
Josh's injury-free years are presented as lived experience, not clinical proof.
A suggested shot list makes his footage directly comparable with the athlete lessons.
Learners can film themselves now and re-film after 6–8 weeks to see their own progress.
